transcript.answer:
Summary — root cause
- The NotReady pods were caused by the application hitting the OS file-descriptor limit (Errno 24: Too many open files). Once the process could no longer accept connections, the readiness probe returned errors (connection refused → HTTP 503) and kubelet marked the container(s) Unready.
- Confirmed facts:
  - Affected pods (all running APP_VERSION=1.4.2, image python:3.12-alpine): 
    - ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 (node: rcabench-worker2) — Ready=false, ContainersReady=false. startTime 2026-10-07T09:44:12Z; Ready transitioned to False at 2026-10-07T09:45:38Z.
    - ledger-api-866db84748-cz4wp (node: rcabench-worker2) — Ready=false, ContainersReady=false. startTime 2026-10-07T09:44:11Z; Ready False at 2026-10-07T09:45:37Z.
    - ledger-api-866db84748-vv6jk (node: rcabench-worker2) — Ready=false, ContainersReady=false. startTime 2026-10-07T09:44:12Z; Ready False at 2026-10-07T09:45:38Z.
  - Other replicas on rcabench-worker were Ready (md6xh, r5mbh, xzjxb on rcabench-worker are Ready=true), so half the replica set (3/6) became NotReady.
  - Application logs (last 1 hour, showing 22 lines per pod) contain repeated errors starting ~2026-10-07T09:45:33Z:
    - "2026-10-07T09:45:33Z ERROR ledger-api accept failed: [Errno 24] Too many open files"
    - repeated every ~10s thereafter.
  - Pod events/readiness failures:
    - Initial readiness probe failures were connection refused (when process still starting).
    - Immediately after the Too many open files errors appeared, readiness probe failures changed to: "HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503" and kubelet logged ContainersNotReady.
  - Deployment: ledger-api rolled to APP_VERSION=1.4.2; ReplicaSet created 6 pods, readyReplicas reported 3 (3 available / 6 updated).
  - Affected node rcabench-worker2 is Ready and shows no memory/disk/PID pressure in node conditions; it hosts the 3 NotReady pods.

Why this caused NotReady
- The application process failed accept() with Errno 24 (too many open files). When the server cannot accept or handle connections it returns 503 on the /healthz check (or fails to accept), which triggers Kubernetes readiness failures (ContainersNotReady → Pod Ready=false). That is the direct chain: FD exhaustion → accept() errors → health endpoint fails → kubelet marks pod NotReady.

Possible root-level causes (ranked)
1. Application regression in 1.4.2 (most likely): a file-descriptor leak or change in connection handling that opens sockets/FDs and doesn't close them, causing per-process FD exhaustion within minutes after startup.
2. Node or container FD limit too low for this workload (less likely given only pods on one node are impacted, but still possible if node-level limits or per-process limits differed between nodes).
3. High traffic spike concentrated to the three pods on rcabench-worker2, exhausting FDs before other pods experienced it.
4. Host-level resource exhaustion or other process on rcabench-worker2 consuming many file descriptors (less likely; node shows Ready and no PIDPressure).

What I fetched / examined
- Pod listing for namespace ledger filtered to ledger-api (showing name, READY, STATUS, restarts, image, node, start time).
- Deployment ledger-api (ready/up-to-date/available, image).
- Full JSON for all ledger-api pods (conditions, containers, readiness probe config, env APP_VERSION).
- kubectl describe for three NotReady pods: ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4, -cz4wp, -vv6jk (events included).
- Logs for each of those three pods covering the last 1 hour (limit 500 lines, all results shown — 22 lines each).
- Namespace pod events around the rollout time (readiness failure messages).
- Node description for rcabench-worker2.

Immediate remediation (fast, low-risk)
- Temporarily restore service health:
  1. Roll back the deployment to the previous known-good version (if rollout introduced the regression):
     - kubectl rollout undo deployment/ledger-api -n ledger
     - or kubectl set image deployment/ledger-api api=<previous-image> -n ledger
  2. If rollback is not acceptable, restart only the affected pods to restore capacity quickly (short-term):
     - kubectl delete pod <pod> -n ledger  (kube will recreate). Or scale down then up.
  3. If you want to preserve 1.4.2 while triaging, cordon the node and drain to move other pods off rcabench-worker2 temporarily:
     - kubectl cordon rcabench-worker2
     - kubectl drain rcabench-worker2 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
     (Note: draining will evict other pods — use with caution.)

Next-best troubleshooting steps (confirm root cause)
- On an affected pod (example ledger-api-...-2zjp4):
  - Inspect process file-descriptor usage inside the container:
    - kubectl exec -n ledger ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 -- sh -c 'ls /proc/1/fd | wc -l'
    - kubectl exec -n ledger ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 -- sh -c 'cat /proc/1/limits'  (shows "Max open files" per-process limit)
  - Check for sockets specifically:
    - kubectl exec -n ledger <pod> -- sh -c 'ss -s' or 'ls -la /proc/1/fd | grep socket | wc -l' (may require ss installed in container; you can run a debug pod on the node to examine host processes)
- On the node rcabench-worker2 (host-level checks; requires node access/SSH or debug pod with hostPID/hostMounts):
  - Check system-wide fd usage:
    - cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nr
    - ss -s
    - lsof -nP | wc -l
  - Per-process FD counts for containerd processes or the python process:
    - Find container PID: crictl ps / docker/ctr commands or from containerID in pod status → then ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l
- Compare with a healthy pod on rcabench-worker to see differences in FD counts and limits.
- Search application code / 1.4.2 changelog for changes that open file/socket handles (database connections, long-lived sockets, file logging handles, etc.).

Longer-term fixes
- If this is an app bug in 1.4.2:
  - Fix the FD leak and release a patch (recommended).
  - Add instrumentation and alerting for FD usage and health: expose open-fd metric and set alert on >80% of limit.
  - Improve graceful degradation / health-check logic so that transient FD pressure doesn't immediately return 503 while still allowing the process to continue handling traffic when safe.
- If the app legitimately needs more descriptors under load:
  - Increase per-process limits on the node (ulimit -n) and system file-max (sysctl fs.file-max). Note: changing container ulimits requires changing host/runtimes or using privileged init steps — document exact platform steps before changing.
- Add resource requests/limits for the pods if missing (current pods are BestEffort — no CPU/memory requests), to improve scheduling and observability and to reduce noisy-neighbor effects.
- Consider readiness probe tuning (longer timeout or a probe endpoint that checks app can actually serve rather than simply open a socket), but only as a secondary measure — this hides the symptom, not the leak.

Concrete commands (safe to run, read-only) to run now
- Verify pod readiness and events (already done, but quick check):
  - kubectl get pods -n ledger -o wide
  - kubectl describe pod <affected-pod> -n ledger
- Check current open files inside a pod:
  - kubectl exec -n ledger ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 -- sh -c 'cat /proc/1/limits | grep \"open files\" -A1; ls /proc/1/fd | wc -l'
- Check container logs for the error (already inspected):
  - kubectl logs -n ledger ledger-api-866db84748-2zjp4 --since=1h

Recommended next actions I can perform (tell me which you want me to run)
- Run the in-pod FD checks (ls /proc/1/fd, cat /proc/1/limits) for one healthy and one unhealthy pod to compare.
- Run a node-level check (cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nr) — requires node access; I can run a debugging pod with host namespace if you permit it.
- Roll back the deployment now (I can provide the exact kubectl command and perform it if you want).
- Restart only the NotReady pods now to restore availability temporarily.

Short conclusion
- Root cause: the ledger-api process in release 1.4.2 hit the process file-descriptor limit (Errno 24), causing accept() failures and readiness probe failures → kubelet marked 3 pods on rcabench-worker2 NotReady (half the replica set). The most likely immediate fix is to roll back 1.4.2 or patch the app to fix the FD leak; temporary mitigation is to restart affected pods or raise FD limits on the host if the app legitimately needs more descriptors.

If you want, I’ll run the in-pod FD checks now (compare a NotReady pod on rcabench-worker2 vs a Ready pod on rcabench-worker) and report exact counts and limits. Which action would you like next?
